interrogate

/in-TERR-uh-gayt/ - the stress falls on TERR · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Interrogate means to question someone or something closely and thoroughly.

Editors at the fact desk interrogate every statistic before it reaches print.

Example

When the bridge's strain gauges disagreed, the engineering team interrogated the data for a week: every sensor's history pulled, every calibration date checked, every spike matched against the maintenance calendar — until the flaw stood exposed, one gauge wired backward on installation day.

Interrogate earns its force here: the data was not skimmed but pressed with question after question, systematically, until it gave up its answer. Examine would be gentler; grill is for people under pressure; interrogate suits a thorough, relentless questioning of anything — a person, a dataset, or an account.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

grill: Grill is the informal, kitchen-table word for questioning someone hard — reporters grill a coach, parents grill a curfew-breaker. Interrogate does the same relentless work in official dress: systematic, sustained, often on the record. A detective interrogates a suspect; a roommate merely grills you.

question: To question someone is the plain, neutral act, at any intensity — one query or fifty. Interrogate marks the far end of that scale: closely, thoroughly, at length, each answer pressed for more. All interrogating is questioning; most questioning never comes near interrogation.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

believe: to take an account on trust, no questions asked

accept: to let a claim pass unchallenged

Where it sits · how sustained and pressing the questioning gets — ask → quiz → interrogate

ask vs. interrogate: To ask is the gentlest form of questioning — one question, no pressure — far milder than interrogate.

quiz vs. interrogate: To quiz someone goes further than asking, firing quick questions in a row, but it stops short of interrogate, which is systematic, sustained, and pressing.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — inter-

Prefix — inter-: between, among

Root — rog

Root — rog: to ask (Latin rogare)

Suffix — -ate

Suffix — -ate: to make, to do

Put it together

Put it together: Inter- (between) + rog (to ask, Latin rogare) + -ate = to ask back and forth between two people — the questioner pressing, the answerer answering, again and again. The rhythm of exchange built into the prefix is why an interrogation never means just one polite question.

Use the root in a new word: prerogative

Use the root in a new word: prerogative: Choosing the season's first movie is the birthday kid's prerogative in our house.

Word Choice

formal / forceful

Interrogate is questioning at full pressure — systematic, sustained, often official. It points outward at a person, a dataset, or an account; scrutinize, its neighbor in this unit, does the same relentless work with the eyes instead of with questions.
